newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China corn exports seen back on the drawing board.
newsitem.headline: China corn exports seen back on the drawing board.

text.p: Politics, not economics, will be the major factor behind any decision that China's grain gurus make on whether or not to export corn, Far East traders said on Wednesday.

Word that central authorities could grant permission for corn-growing provinces to export between 1.5 and 2.5 million tonnes of new crop early in 1997 could not be immediately confirmed as China's National Day holiday continued.
Traders in Hong Kong, Singapore and South Korea said Chinese corn was currently too expensive, and that buyers in the region were covered to year-end, some even through to mid-1997.
Export licences, if granted, would not be used before early 1997, and sales would be kept to a minimum, traders said.

"The provinces will export just a small amount and it will be because if they export nothing they might not get licences the following year," one Hong Kong source said, adding he thought exports would be capped at 300,000 tonnes.
He expected Chinese corn prices to remain higher than competing exporters, forcing provincial authorities to subsidise any exports -- and thus encouraging them to keep sales low.
Grain bureaux borrowed to purchase grain from farmers, and would have to borrow further to subsidise exports if domestic prices did not align with world prices, traders said.
A fear of fuelling inflation could also dampen enthusiasm for exports, as it did this year, they said.
Chinese corn is now 1,370 yuan ($165) per tonne FOB (free on board) at the northern port of Dalian. Freight and the quality spread would add another $15, traders said.
U.S. corn is currently arriving in Far East ports priced around US$156 cost and freight, traders said.
The crop currently being harvested in the northern provinces of Jilin, Heilongjiang and Liaoning could be as high as 120 million tonnes, trade and industry sources have said.
Official figures put 1995 corn production at 101 million tonnes. Annual demand is about 115 million.
This would give China a bumper 1996/97 crop, adding to reserves said to be 30 million tonnes, and could bring some pressure to bear on prices over the next few months.

But China could be on the same path it followed in the first half of 1996, when corn stocks were high, domestic prices low, and grain bureaux and traders eager to export -- yet no green light came from central authorities in Beijing.
As a result, two million tonnes of corn shipped to Dalian around April and May when the opportunity to earn huge export dollars was greatest are now rotting, traders said.
To avoid the same waste in 1997, the sources said, China should be confident enough in its domestic supply to play the markets and take advantage of price spreads.

"The best thing China could do is export three million tonnes of corn in the first half of the year (1997), push the CBOT (Chicago Board of Trade) price down and at the same time, buy for delivery late in the year," one trader said.

"This way they make money for imports and release stock from this year's crop. They meet demand in the south and relieve the transportation system that prevents them getting their own corn to where it is needed," he said.
"But they can't coordinate themselves because of the bureaucracy, there are just too many players. So they missed the chance this year, and they'll miss it next year," he said.
"China could have done this in June and July this year and made a lot of money. But it is a political, not an economic decision, so we can't say if it is right or wrong," he said.
-- Hong Kong newsroom (852) 2843-6470
